meta.note: Official rules and rates are quoted from sources fetched and read from their official publishers on the retrieval date recorded for each source (2026-11-07 through 2026-11-13; the load-bearing subset was re-read live on 2026-11-13). Private lease, ledger, license, and coverage facts are not independently verified. Dollar amounts are conditional scenario arithmetic using the owner-brief amounts, not certified lawful maxima or permission to serve notice. Unsupported official-confirmation cells are blank and flagged. Tenant names and initials are replaced with placeholders; supplied dates and dollar amounts are unchanged. This is a research summary, not legal advice.

sources.title: Sec. 37.15 — Reporting Obligations; Licensing (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote: (a) Owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37 shall be required to report certain information about their units to the Rent Board … (e) If a landlord has substantially complied with the obligation to report information about a rental unit as required under this Section 37.15, the landlord shall receive a license to impose rent increases on tenants in that unit under Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2). If the landlord has not substantially complied with the reporting obligation, then the license to impose rent increases shall be temporarily suspended during the period of the landlord's noncompliance … but a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension. (c) For units (other than condominium units) in buildings with 10 units or more, the information described in subsection (b) shall be reported to the Rent Board by July 1, 2022, and updated by March 1, 2023 and annually by March 1 of each successive year. For condominium units and units in buildings with fewer than 10 units, the information shall be reported commencing March 1, 2023 and updated annually by March 1 of each successive year. … [Added by Ord. No. 265-20, effective January 18, 2021]
sources.used_for: The rent increase licence: who must hold it, how it is obtained, and the consequence of not holding it.

sources.title: Sec. 37.3 — Rent Limitations (S.F. Admin. Code ch. 37)
sources.quote: (a)(1) Annual Rent Increase. On March 1 of each year, the Board shall publish the increase in the CPI … A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase. In no event, however, shall the allowable annual increase be greater than 7%. … (b)(5) Nonconforming Rent Increases. Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this section shall be null and void. … (a)(11)(A) … a landlord may not impose increases solely because a tenant has added an additional occupant to an existing tenancy … notwithstanding a rental agreement or lease that specifically permits a rent increase for additional occupants.
sources.used_for: The annual allowance, the 7% ceiling, the licence condition written into the ordinance, notice contents, the null-and-void rule, and the additional-occupant prohibition.

sources.title: The Rent Board Housing Inventory — and the rent increase licence
sources.quote: All owners of residential property are required to report … Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license that allows them to impose annual allowable and banked rent increases. … Deadline: March 1 of every year. You can still make a Housing Inventory submission and receive a rent increase license after the deadline. However, your rent increase notice will not be enforceable without having a rent increase license on the effective date of the notice. … a landlord must have a current rent increase license on file with the Rent Board before any annual or banked rent increase can go into effect. The rent increase license does not need to be included with your rent increase notice. … Reporting is free. For units (other than condominiums) in buildings with 10 units or more, the law became operative on July 1, 2022. Reporting requirements began March 1, 2023 for condominiums and units in buildings with fewer than 10 units.
sources.used_for: Individual-owner reporting duty, automatic license generation after reporting, late submission, annual deadline, effective-date gate, and no need to attach the license to notice.

sources.title: Banked rent increases
sources.quote: A landlord may raise the rent once every 12 months by the allowed annual increase. … A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase. If less than 24 months pass, the skipped increase is lost and cannot be imposed at a later date. … Banked increases do not have to be approved by the Rent Board, but must be calculated correctly. They cannot be compounded or prorated. … There is no limit on how much can be banked. … Notice posted November 9, 2026: If enacted as currently proposed, the legislation would apply to banked rent increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026, and capital improvement rent increases based on petitions filed with the Rent Board on or after September 15, 2026. This legislation has not been enacted and is subject to change.
sources.used_for: Banking: the 24-month no-increase statement, partial increases, no Board approval, no compounding, and notice contents. Read with Rule 4.12(a), which measures 12 months from when the skipped allowance became available (H-01).

sources.title: Learn about rent increases in San Francisco
sources.quote: The allowed rent increase percentage in San Francisco is 1.6%. The percentage is effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. … Notice: Proposed Changes to Rent Increase Limitations — Posted November 9, 2026 … If enacted as currently proposed, the legislation would apply to banked rent increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026, and capital improvement rent increases based on petitions filed with the Rent Board on or after September 15, 2026. This legislation has not been enacted and is subject to change. … A landlord can impose the first annual increase 12 months after the date the tenant's lease began. … 90-day written notice if the increase (either by itself or combined with another increase in the same year) is more than 10% … Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar. … A landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new (or additional) roommate has moved into a tenant's unit.
sources.used_for: Current rate, first/annual timing, base-rent calculation, notice periods, no rounding, and additional occupants. Official worked-example year labels contain errors cross-checked against Form 571 (H-19). Also confirms the November 9, 2026 proposed-changes warning and its September 15 notice date (H-22).

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part IV — §§4.10 (Notice) and 4.12 (Banking)
sources.quote: §4.12(a) … the rent may be increased only one time every twelve (12) months … A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up … §4.12(b) … failure to include such information shall not render the increase null and void. §4.10(b) Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this Section shall render the entire rent increase null and void, unless the amount requested equals no more than the allowable annual and banked rent increase(s).
sources.used_for: Rule 4.12(a): 12 months from when the skipped allowance could have been imposed; non-compounding/no rounding; Rule 4.12(b) banked-date itemisation and its express non-void provision; Rule 4.10(b) text-specific exception (H-15).

sources.title: File #261020 — Administrative Code - Cap On Rent Increases for Rent-Controlled Units
sources.quote: Ordinance amending the Administrative Code to provide that banked rent increases and capital improvement rent increases for rent-controlled units may not increase a tenant's rent by more than a total of 10% per year, for the next three years; and making various non-substantive changes. Type: Ordinance. Status: Pending Committee Action. Introduced: 9/15/2026. In control: Land Use and Transportation Committee. Final action: (none). Enactment date: (none). … Proposed §37.3(h) (Leg Ver1): may not impose banked rent increases under Section 37.3(a)(2), and/or rent increases based on any of the types of capital improvements described in Section 37.3(a)(3), that cause a tenant's rent to increase by more than a total of 10% of the lowest base rent that was in effect at any time during the 12 months immediately preceding the date the increase takes effect … This 10% limit shall apply to banked rent increases based on rent increase notices provided on or after September 15, 2026 … and shall remain in effect until December 31, 2029 unless extended by ordinance. A landlord may accumulate rent increases exceeding 10% per year … and may impose such increases to take effect on or after January 1, 2030 … Proposed §37.15(b)(2)(F): whether any banked rent increases were imposed under Section 37.3(a)(2) during the previous 12 months.
sources.used_for: Proposed cap and Housing Inventory banked-reporting amendment; Legistar detail and Leg Ver1/Leg Dig Ver1 re-checked 2026-11-10. Rent Board notices on S04 and S05 warn of proposed retroactive application to banked notices provided on or after September 15, 2026 if enacted as proposed.

sources.title: Rent Increases Under Section 6.14 and Costa-Hawkins
sources.quote: Rules and Regulations Section 6.14 provides for an unlimited rent increase on remaining occupants when the last original occupant vacates the unit, as long as the landlord timely served all remaining occupants with a written "6.14 notice." … The 6.14 notice must be served on each subsequent occupant within a reasonable time after the landlord knows or should have known of the occupancy. Generally, sixty days is considered reasonable. A 6.14 notice can be served on any subsequent occupant, whether the subsequent occupant is a subtenant or a co-tenant. … In addition, a co-tenant, as opposed to a subtenant, is not subject to such a rent increase, regardless of when the co-tenant moved in. A co-tenant is someone who has an oral or written agreement with the landlord, or who has become a tenant by the conduct of the parties such as the landlord's acceptance of rent.
sources.used_for: What an occupant change does and does not allow: the §6.14 notice, the sixty-day reasonableness benchmark, and the co-tenant versus subtenant distinction.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part VI — §6.14 Establishing Rental Rates for Subsequent Occupants
sources.level: Local — Rent Board rules and regulations
sources.quote: §6.14(b) Co-occupants who commenced occupancy before, on or after January 1, 1996: Failure to give such a notice within 60 days of the landlord's actual knowledge of the occupancy by the subsequent occupant(s) establishes a rebuttable presumption that notice was not given within a reasonable period of time. … §6.14(c) Subsequent Occupants who are not Co-occupants and who commenced occupancy on or after January 1, 1996, where the last Original Occupant vacated on or after April 25, 2000: … unless the subsequent occupant proves that the landlord waived his or her right to increase the rent by … (2) Failing, within 90 days of receipt of written notice … or actual knowledge that the last original occupant no longer permanently resides at the unit … to serve written notice of a rent increase or a reservation of the right to increase the rent at a later date … §6.14(d)(2) The landlord is entitled to establish a new base rent under the Costa Hawkins Rental Housing Act, California Civil Code Section 1954.53(d), even if no notice was served on the subsequent occupant(s).
sources.used_for: Distinguishes §6.14(b) (co-occupants: 60-day initial notice presumption), §6.14(c) (non-co-occupants where last original occupant vacates on or after April 25, 2000: 90-day post-vacancy reservation/waiver window), and Costa-Hawkins under Civil Code §1954.53(d).

sources.title: Petition for a Determination Pursuant to Section 6.14 and/or Costa-Hawkins
sources.quote: A landlord is not required to file a petition with the Rent Board for approval of a rent increase pursuant to Section 6.14 or Costa-Hawkins Section 1954.53(d). However, if a landlord is unsure whether a rent increase is justified, the landlord may file a petition at the Rent Board to seek a determination that either or both sections authorize a rent increase. … Finally, Section 6.14 requires the last original occupant to "vacate" the unit, while Costa-Hawkins only requires the last original occupant to no longer "permanently reside" in the unit.
sources.used_for: That no pre-filing is required, that an optional determination petition exists, and the vacate versus permanently-reside distinction.

sources.title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations, Part XIII — §13.14 Licensing – Notice of Rent Increase
sources.quote: Any rent increase under Ordinance Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2) purporting to be effective while the landlord is unlicensed shall render the entire rent increase null and void; provided, however, that the effective date of the rent increase, not the date of service, shall be used to determine whether or not the increase conforms with the provisions of this section. Nothing in this Regulation shall affect a landlord's banking rights or the ability to accumulate otherwise lawful rent increases that were found to be null and void. … with respect to condominium units and buildings with less than ten residential units, this section shall only apply to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2023. This section shall apply to all rent increases that are effective on or after July 1, 2022, except that with respect to condominium units and buildings with less than ten residential units, this section shall only apply to rent increases that are effective on or after March 1, 2023.
sources.used_for: The adopted regulation that the effective date (not the service date) governs licensing, and that an unlicensed null-and-void increase does not forfeit banking rights.

licensing_steps.question: Does a single individual owner (no corporation) need a rent increase licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The duty is written for "owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37" and the Housing Inventory page states that all owners of residential property must report, including units in buildings with fewer than 10 units and condominiums. There is no small-owner or individual-owner exemption.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence an application that the Rent Board approves?
licensing_steps.answer: No. It is generated automatically when the owner reports the unit in the Housing Inventory with a tenant in occupancy: "Property owners who report that a unit is tenant-occupied will receive a rent increase license". Reporting is free and is done online in the Rent Board Portal. No approval, hearing or fee is involved.

licensing_steps.question: Does the owner have to send the Rent Board the rent increase notice, or ask permission for the annual or banked increase?
licensing_steps.answer: No. Annual and banked increases within the ordinance limits are imposed by the owner: banked increases "do not have to be approved by the Rent Board". The Board-facing duty is the reporting duty, and the annual report includes the base rent (in $250 increments) and occupancy. Board involvement is required only for an increase above the allowance, which needs a landlord petition, and for any tenant challenge.

licensing_steps.question: When must the licence exist?
licensing_steps.answer: A current licence must be on file before any annual or banked increase "can go into effect". It does not have to be attached to the notice, but it must be live on the effective date. Adopted Rule §13.14 states the gate expressly: the effective date, not the date of service, determines whether the increase conforms. The reporting deadline is 1 March every year; for a building with fewer than 10 units, reporting began on 1 March 2023.

licensing_steps.question: What happens if the unit was never reported?
licensing_steps.answer: The licence is "temporarily suspended" while the owner is not in compliance; it is restored prospectively once the information is filed, but the tenant is not obligated to pay the increased rent for the months during the suspension. Rule §13.14 adds that an unlicensed increase is null and void yet "Nothing in this Regulation shall affect a landlord's banking rights or the ability to accumulate otherwise lawful rent increases that were found to be null and void." That is the precise mechanism that makes an otherwise lawful increase challengeable — and it is cured by filing, not by anything in the notice.

licensing_steps.question: Is the licence the same thing as the annual Rent Board fee?
licensing_steps.answer: No. The licence is free and comes from the Housing Inventory report. The fee is separate: $59.00 per dwelling unit for the 2026-2027 tax year, due 1 March, of which up to $29.50 may be recovered from tenants. For the 2027 Rent Board fee (due 1 March 2027), the Rent Board states a December 14, 2026 deadline to submit a Request for Exemption. Requesting a fee exemption does not satisfy the Housing Inventory requirement.

licensing_steps.question: Can a tenant check whether the owner holds a licence?
licensing_steps.answer: Yes. The Rent Board states that a tenant can search the Rent Board Portal to see whether the landlord is up to date, by address or Assessor's Parcel Number, and can check whether a licence was on file on the effective date. The Housing Inventory information reported by owners is public. If there was no licence, the tenant may file a Tenant Petition for Unlawful Rent Increase after the effective date, or a Tenant Summary Petition before it, and may be entitled to a rent refund for an unlicensed increase that took effect.

licensing_steps.question: Is the Rent Board licence the only licence an individual owner needs?
licensing_steps.answer: No — there is a second, separate City registration that is often confused with it. The Business Registration Certificate is issued by the Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector, not the Rent Board, and it is a general business-tax registration. It is unrelated to whether a rent increase is lawful, and holding or not holding it does not affect the rent increase licence.

licensing_steps.question: Does this owner need a Business Registration Certificate?
licensing_steps.answer: On the reported facts, probably not. The Tax Collector states that a person receiving rental income from "one residential structure consisting of fewer than four units" is "not, by reason of that fact alone, required to obtain a business registration certificate", and lists the same carve-out among its registration triggers. Two units in one building is fewer than four. The same page states that such a lessor need not file a Gross Receipts return unless they lease four or more units in an individual building.

licensing_steps.question: When would a Business Registration Certificate become required?
licensing_steps.answer: The exemption is expressly conditional. The Tax Collector warns that "if the same person engages in other business activities or incurs payroll expense, a business registration certificate may be required", and short-term residential rental income requires registration "regardless of the amount". The determination also depends on the actual unit count in the building, which the Tax Collector is authorised to decide. This is logged as flag H-21 and must be confirmed against the owner's own facts and, if needed, the Tax Collector's Help Center.

process_steps.detail: Built 1940, so the date test in the Rent Ordinance is met on its face (units built on or before 13 June 1979). Confirm the unit is not in an exempt category and record the certificate-of-occupancy date.

Complete or update the Housing Inventory for both units and confirm each generated license. Best practice is to do this before serving notice; the official hard gate is licensure on the increase’s effective date. Save dated evidence and recheck on that date.

process_steps.action: Fix the base rent and the anniversary date from records
process_steps.detail: Use the lease and full rent ledger, not a lease-start amount alone. Unit 1’s $3,995.00 is reported again on April 1, 2026. Unit 2’s $3,150.00 is supplied only as the June 1, 2019 lease-start rent; its current base rent is unverified. Check fixed-term clauses and all passthroughs.

process_steps.action: Add up the allowance, without compounding or rounding
process_steps.detail: Current published annual allowance is 1.6%. If the ledger establishes unused allowances, add them without compounding or rounding up. Unit 2’s 13.1% is a conditional illustration: six potentially banked components (11.5%) plus current 1.6%, all on the unverified $3,150.00 scenario input.

process_steps.action: Pick the effective date and work backwards
process_steps.detail: One increase every 12 months. 30 days' notice if the increase is 10% or less; 90 days if more; plus 5 days if mailed. The 1.6% rate expires on 28 Feb 2027.

process_steps.action: Write the notice with the itemisation
process_steps.detail: Dollar amount, percentage, effective date, which part is the annual increase and which part is banked, and the dates the banked amount is based on.

Use personal delivery or mail under Civil Code §827 and Code of Civil Procedure §1013. For California-to-California mail plan on five extra calendar days; longer extensions apply in other circumstances. Keep dated proof.
Report into the Housing Inventory by 1 March each year so the licence never lapses; pay the $59.00 per-unit fee separately if it applies.

notice_rows.item: In writing, delivered to the tenant
notice_rows.detail: Personal delivery, or mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013 (adds 5 days).

notice_rows.item: At least 30 days before the effective date (increase of 10% or less)
notice_rows.detail: Unit 1 (1.6% or 3.0%) falls in this band.

notice_rows.item: At least 90 days before the effective date (increase over 10%)

notice_rows.detail: Use the percentage in force on that date, not the one in force when the notice is written.

notice_rows.item: Which portion is the annual increase and which is banked
notice_rows.detail: Required by the ordinance, on or before the date the notice is given.

notice_rows.item: The dates on which a banked amount is based
notice_rows.detail: Rule 4.12(b); omitting this does not void the increase under the rule, but §37.3(b)(5) makes any nonconforming increase null and void — so include it (flag H-15).

notice_rows.item: No rounding up and no compounding
notice_rows.detail: Arithmetic shown on the notice must match the published percentages exactly.

notice_rows.item: No charge for the April 2026 occupant change
notice_rows.detail: An additional occupant cannot support a rent increase, even if a lease says otherwise.

reasons.reason: The Rent Board's published annual allowance (1.6%)
reasons.detail: The ordinance is a price-control scheme: no justification letter is needed for the annual portion.
Itemise the years and percentages; add, never compound.

reasons.reason: Certified capital improvements or operating-and-maintenance costs
reasons.lawful: Only with a Rent Board petition
reasons.detail: An increase above the allowance requires a landlord petition; certified O&M increases are capped at 7%.

Not a unilateral annual/banked justification. Valid banked amounts can exceed the current annual allowance without a petition; any separate comparables or other petition route is fact-specific and no supporting facts are supplied.
Expressly prohibited, even where the lease provides for it.
Bad-faith pressure to vacate exposes the owner to treble damages and attorney's fees.

reasons.reason: After the tenant complained about repairs or habitability
reasons.lawful: Review required — not an automatic 180-day bar
reasons.detail: Retaliatory purpose and statutory conditions control. Section 1942.5 lists protected activity and 180-day events but preserves lawful cause and contains a good-faith-ground provision. Screen the history; do not describe every increase in that window as automatically unlawful.

reasons.reason: A rent produced by pricing software
reasons.detail: Algorithmic devices using non-public competitor data are prohibited in San Francisco.

practice_rows.corporate: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules.
practice_rows.individual: Same ordinance, same percentage, same notice rules — no small-owner exemption in Chapter 37.

practice_rows.corporate: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report.
practice_rows.individual: Required, obtained from the annual Housing Inventory report; free and automatic.

practice_rows.corporate: Banned in San Francisco: no algorithmic device using non-public competitor data to set rents or occupancy.
practice_rows.individual: Banned as well; the prohibition is on "a landlord", and tenants and tenant nonprofits may sue.

practice_rows.corporate: DOJ allegations and a proposed RealPage settlement document concerns about shared nonpublic competitor data in portfolio-scale pricing tools; they do not establish typical behavior by every corporate landlord.
practice_rows.individual: No official dataset measures how individual SF owners set increases. The verified statement is the rule set, not a behavioural average.

practice_rows.corporate: The AB 1482 exemption for single-family homes and condominiums is unavailable to a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member.
practice_rows.individual: An individual owner may qualify for that exemption — but it is irrelevant to these units, which are already under SF's lower local cap.

practice_rows.topic: Records that make an increase defensible
practice_rows.corporate: No official source establishes a universal corporate recordkeeping practice. A documented per-unit ledger, neutral policy, notice, and service evidence are prudent controls.
practice_rows.individual: Use the same per-unit evidence discipline: lease, full ledger, license evidence, coverage, calculation, notice, and proof of service. This is a recommended checklist, not an exhaustive statement of every legal duty.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a difference between the two units itself unlawful?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No provision in the cited Chapter 37, Civil Code §1947.12, Government Code §12955 or the federal Fair Housing Act requires identical treatment. The prohibition is discrimination or harassment because of a protected characteristic.

Federal: race, colour, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, disability. California adds, among others, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, marital status, ancestry, source of income, veteran or military status, and genetic information.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is a discriminatory rent increase already harassment under local law?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Yes: §37.10B(a)(9) makes it bad-faith harassment to "violate any law which prohibits discrimination" in the protected categories it lists.

fair_housing_rows.point: What objective reasons justify different outcomes for the two units?
fair_housing_rows.finding: Use documented lease terms, verified current base rent, anniversary dates, and proven banked history. The brief supplies different lease-start dates and amounts, but Unit 2’s current base and both units’ complete histories are not verified.

Selecting a unit because of a protected characteristic; bad-faith pressure to vacate; retaliation under the conditions of Civil Code §1942.5; unresolved repair petitions; or a nonconforming notice. A 180-day complaint history is a review trigger, not an automatic bar.

fair_housing_rows.point: Is there an official safe-harbour rule for "treat both units the same"?
fair_housing_rows.finding: No official source states that raising both units identically cures a discrimination risk, or that raising one unit creates one. Both questions are decided on the reason for the difference, not on the pattern.

review_rows.test: Is the unit covered by Chapter 37?
review_rows.evidence: Certificate of occupancy / year built 1940; not an exempt category.

review_rows.test: Does the owner hold a current rent increase licence?
review_rows.evidence: Rent Board Portal licence status, dated.

review_rows.test: Is the percentage the one in force on the effective date?
Was the increase applied to base rent only?
review_rows.evidence: No passthroughs bundled in; utilities/parking documented.

review_rows.test: Is the arithmetic additive, not compounded, and not rounded up?
review_rows.evidence: Arithmetic only: U1 $63.92 annual-only; U2 $412.65 for the conditional 13.1% scenario. Private base and history remain unverified.

review_rows.test: Does the lease permit an increase now, and has at least 12 months elapsed?
review_rows.evidence: Read Unit 1’s April 2026 instrument for fixed term and escalation clause; verify both ledgers and last increase dates. Lease-start dates alone are insufficient.

review_rows.test: Does the banked amount satisfy the banking test?
review_rows.evidence: Both measuring points are satisfied by the conditional February 1, 2027 Unit 1 scenario: 24 months without an increase and 12 months since the skipped allowance became available. Verify the actual ledger; do not treat the two formulations as a proven conflict.

review_rows.test: Is the notice period long enough, including 5 days for mail?
review_rows.evidence: 30 days for U1; 90 days for U2's 13.1%.

review_rows.test: Does the notice itemise annual vs banked, with dates?
review_rows.evidence: Draft notice attached to the record.

review_rows.test: Is any part of the increase retaliatory?
review_rows.evidence: Screen §1942.5 protected activity and listed events in the prior 180 days, other protected activity at any time, rent status, lawful cause, repairs, and any good-faith ground. No blanket clearance can be given from public facts.

review_rows.test: Is any part of the increase discriminatory or intended to push the tenant out?
review_rows.evidence: Written policy: same calculation method for both units; no vacancy-related motive; no pricing software.

review_rows.test: Can the tenant verify the number without a lawyer?
review_rows.evidence: Recommended: notice names the rate period, Rent Board phone number, petition route, and official referral resources. Do not promise free representation.

review_rows.test: Is any required repair or tenant petition unresolved?
review_rows.evidence: Review written repair requests, inspections, notices of violation, and any pending petition. A qualifying Failure to Repair and Maintain petition is due no later than 60 days after receipt of the increase notice.

review_rows.test: If occupants changed, was a proper §6.14 notice served, and is an original occupant still in the unit?
review_rows.evidence: The April 2026 change documents; any 6.14 notice and proof of service; the agreement showing co-tenant or subtenant status.

review_rows.test: Has proposed File #261020 changed before a banked increase is noticed or imposed?
review_rows.evidence: Re-read the Rent Board warning and Legistar final text/status. The 2026-11-09 agency warning says the proposal would cover banked increases noticed on or after 2026-09-15; early service is not a verified workaround.

flags.item: Banking guidance uses two measuring points; worked-example labels need care
flags.detail: Rule 4.12(a) reads in full: "A landlord who refrains from imposing an annual rent increase, or any portion thereof, may accumulate said increase and impose that amount on or after the tenant's subsequent rent increase anniversary date; however, the rent may be increased only one time every twelve (12) months. This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase. Only those increases which could have been imposed on, or subsequent to, April 1, 1982, may be accumulated. A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up". The Rent Board's banking guidance page uses a different measuring point: "A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase." Re-fetched 2026-11-08. For a tenancy reviewed annually both tests are satisfied by the Unit 1 scenario date, so this is not a proven legal conflict; the two formulations measure from different events.
flags.effect: The 1.4% component is not conditional on choosing between two rules. It remains conditional on the actual lease, anniversary, license, and ledger. Official worked-example year errors are separately logged H-19.
flags.action: Apply Rule 4.12(a) and the guidance together. Note the additional clause "This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase", which is why banked amounts are combined with an annual increase rather than served alone. Verify dates from the ledger, not from the Rent Board's worked-example year labels (see H-19).

flags.item: Unit 1 anniversary and prior-increase history are not verified
flags.detail: February 1, 2027 is a scenario based on the February 1, 2025 lease start and no intervening increase. The April 1, 2026 paperwork and full ledger were not supplied for review.
flags.effect: Any different last-increase date changes the anniversary, available bank, and notice calendar.
flags.action: Review the 2025 lease, April 2026 instrument, every later notice, and the complete rent ledger.

flags.item: Unit 2 zero-prior-increase assumption is not supplied or verified
flags.detail: The 13.1% illustration assumes no increase after June 1, 2019. That is an assumption made for arithmetic, not an established owner statement or official fact.
flags.effect: Any prior increase changes the base, bank, anniversary, and notice threshold.
flags.action: Produce the full rent ledger and every increase notice since June 2019 before using any banked amount.

flags.item: Rent increase licence status unknown
flags.detail: Whether both units are current in the Housing Inventory was not checked; the record is held in the Rent Board Portal, which this session cannot access.
flags.effect: Without a licence on the effective date the increase is unenforceable and the tenant may not owe the increase for the suspension months.
flags.action: Check the Portal and save a dated screenshot before serving.

flags.item: Coverage not confirmed against official records
flags.detail: Year built 1940 satisfies the date test on its face, but coverage also depends on the unit not being in an exempt class (for example certain single-family or condominium situations).
flags.effect: If a unit is not covered, the local cap does not apply and the analysis changes entirely.
flags.action: Check the address on the City Property Information Map and confirm with the Rent Board.

flags.item: Unit 1's April 2026 occupant change needs documentation
flags.detail: The analysis treats 1 April 2026 as a partial change of occupancy (an original tenant remained), so there is no vacancy reset and no additional-occupant charge.
flags.effect: If the original tenant had in fact vacated, Costa-Hawkins could allow a new initial rent — a different result entirely.
flags.action: Keep the 2025 lease, the 2026 change documents, and proof of continuous occupancy.

flags.item: Base rent composition not documented
flags.detail: The increase must be calculated on base rent, which includes housing services such as parking or storage and excludes temporary passthroughs.
flags.effect: A bundled charge in the base rent would change the dollar amount.
flags.action: Confirm what the $3,995.00 and $3,150.00 include.

flags.item: The 2027-28 rate is not published
flags.detail: The 1.6% rate applies only to increases effective 1 March 2026 – 28 February 2027. The next rate is set on 1 March 2027.
flags.effect: Any effective date after 28 February 2027 uses an unknown percentage — left blank, not guessed.
flags.action: Re-check Form 571 after 1 March 2027.

flags.item: Retaliation and repair history require a fact-specific review
flags.detail: Section 1942.5 is not an automatic 180-day prohibition on every increase. It addresses retaliation under stated conditions, preserves lawful cause, and includes a good-faith-ground provision. Separately, a qualifying repair petition can defer an annual increase.
flags.effect: Protected activity, repair requests, inspections, disputes, and petition deadlines can create exposure even when arithmetic is correct.
flags.action: Review correspondence, complaints, inspections, rent status, lawful cause, repairs, and any petitions; obtain legal review if any exist.

flags.item: "Reasonable and normal" market increase for 94122 — no official figure
flags.detail: No official source publishes a permissible or typical market increase for covered units in 94122. Commercial listing data is not an official source and was not used.
flags.effect: The value is left blank. The official ceiling is the only verified number.
flags.action: Treat the Rent Board allowance as the reasonableness benchmark.

flags.item: No official dataset on corporate vs individual owner behaviour
flags.detail: Official sources state the rules that bind every landlord; none measures how individual SF owners typically set increases. The federal 2024 Rental Housing Finance Survey (S34, read 2026-11-13) is national in scope and contains no San Francisco or 94122 owner-behaviour figure; the blank is a verified absence of official data, not an omission.
flags.effect: Practice comparison is qualitative and cited to the ordinance, not to statistics.
flags.action: None required; do not rely on industry averages.

flags.item: Service dates are computed, not official
flags.detail: The dates add the statutory period to the intended effective date, with 5 extra days for mail under Code of Civil Procedure §1013.
flags.effect: Weekends, holidays and proof of service can move the last safe date.
flags.action: Serve well before the last date and keep proof of service.

flags.item: The 13.1% scenario is neither a certified maximum nor a reasonableness finding
flags.detail: The additive arithmetic is reproducible on $3,150.00, but the current base and no-prior-increase premise are unverified. Official banking guidance does not supply a ZIP-specific business recommendation to take the whole amount at once.
flags.effect: The amount may change completely after the ledger review. Any phase-in choice is a separate lawful-neutral business decision, not a legal safe harbour.
flags.action: Do not serve a 13.1% notice from this illustration. Verify all inputs first, then document a neutral decision.

flags.item: Repo defect found and repaired: broken federal statute link
flags.detail: Row S25 in data/sources.csv and docs/sources.html pointed at uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml, which returned "Page Not Found" when fetched on 2026-11-07. Replaced with the HUD Fair Housing Act overview page, which was fetched and reads as quoted.
flags.effect: One prior citation was not verifiable in its published form.
flags.action: Repaired in this session; review the diff.

flags.item: Notice-defect consequences are text-specific, not universally void
flags.detail: Section 37.3(b)(5) states a null-and-void rule. Rule 4.10(b) contains an exception where the amount is no more than allowable annual plus banked increases, and Rule 4.12(b) expressly says omission of banked dates does not itself render the increase null and void.
flags.effect: It is inaccurate to say every itemisation omission automatically voids an otherwise valid increase. The conservative course remains full itemisation.
flags.action: State the annual and banked dollar amounts, percentages, effective date, and banked basis dates; do not rely on an exception.

flags.item: Owner's premise partly incorrect: no per-increase filing with the Rent Board
flags.detail: The owner believed the Rent Board must be informed of, or must license, each increase. The licence is real but comes from the annual Housing Inventory report; annual and banked increases "do not have to be approved by the Rent Board".
flags.effect: The compliance step is the annual report, not a filing about the increase.
flags.action: Report by 1 March each year; serve a conforming notice for each increase.

flags.item: Unit 1 fixed-term versus month-to-month status is unknown
flags.detail: The April 1, 2026 continuing-tenancy instrument was not supplied. Official California guidance says rent cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement permits increases; renewal is another possible point.
flags.effect: A February 1, 2027 increase could be too early. If a fixed term runs through March 31, 2027 without an escalation clause, an April 1, 2027 scenario would use the not-yet-published 2027–28 rate; that rate cell stays blank.
flags.action: Read the signed instrument and any escalation/renewal clause before selecting an effective date.

flags.item: Unit 2 current base rent is not expressly supplied
flags.detail: The brief supplies $3,150.00 as the June 1, 2019 lease-start rent. It does not separately certify that this is the current base rent in November 2026.
flags.effect: The $50.40 annual-only and $412.65 combined figures are illustrations on that input, not verified current amounts or lawful maxima. Official current-base confirmation is blank.
flags.action: Verify the current base rent and its components from the lease and full ledger.

flags.item: Official Rent Board worked examples contain year-label errors
flags.detail: The current rent-increase page includes an example assigning 1.6% to June 1, 2025, and its multiple-year example contains inconsistent year labels. The banking page’s worked example later refers to August 1, 2024 while using the 2025 scenario. Form 571 controls the published periods and rates.
flags.effect: Do not copy example-year labels. The calculations here use Form 571 dates and independently recomputed arithmetic.
flags.action: Use Form 571 for every effective period and recheck the current official page before serving.

flags.item: Free tenant representation is not guaranteed by the referral listing
flags.detail: The Rent Board confirms that a lawyer is not required to file a petition and lists legal resources, including a Sunset office. The listing describes legal assistance and, for some providers, income or service-area limits; it does not promise every tenant free representation for notice review.
flags.effect: Tenants have official review routes, but availability, eligibility, scope, and capacity must be confirmed with each provider.
flags.action: Describe these as referral resources, not guaranteed free lawyers. Rent Board counseling and petitions remain available without counsel.

flags.item: Business Registration Certificate determination is conditional and rests on owner-supplied facts
flags.detail: The sub-four-unit carve-out is written as an exemption from registration "by reason of that fact alone". The Tax Collector expressly warns that "if the same person engages in other business activities or incurs payroll expense, a business registration certificate may be required", that short-term rental income requires registration regardless of amount, and that the Tax Collector "is authorized to determine what constitutes a separate building and the number of units in a building". The two-unit count, the absence of other SF business activity, the absence of payroll expense, and the absence of short-term rental income are all owner-supplied facts and were not independently verified.
flags.effect: If any of those facts differs, a Business Registration Certificate may be required independently of the rent increase. This does not change the rent increase licence analysis, which is separate.
flags.action: Confirm the unit count and the owner's other SF activities; ask the Tax Collector's Help Center in writing before relying on the exemption.

flags.item: Pending ordinance would cap banked increases at 10% per year — re-check before serving any large catch-up
flags.detail: Board of Supervisors File #261020 would add §37.3(h) capping combined banked (§37.3(a)(2)) and capital-improvement (§37.3(a)(3)) increases at 10% per year of the lowest base rent in effect during the preceding 12 months through December 31, 2029 (unless extended), with excess amounts accumulated for imposition on or after January 1, 2030, and would amend §37.15(b)(2)(F) to require Housing Inventory reporting of banked increases imposed in the prior 12 months. Legistar on 2026-11-10 shows Pending Committee Action (Land Use and Transportation Committee; introduced 2026-09-15; Youth Commission response 2026-10-07), no final action and no enactment date: proposed, not law. Re-checked live on Legistar 2026-11-13: still Pending Committee Action in the Land Use and Transportation Committee, no final action and no enactment date. In its November 9, 2026 notice, the Rent Board warns that if enacted as currently proposed it would apply to banked increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026, and capital-improvement petitions filed on or after that date. It is subject to change.
flags.effect: Unit 2's conditional scenario includes 11.5% banked plus a 1.6% annual allowance (13.1% total); the banked component alone exceeds 10%. Unit 2's illustrative 90-day notice dates (November 25 / November 30, 2026) fall on or after September 15, 2026, so any notice served now would fall inside the proposed lookback window if enacted as drafted. The interaction with other charges and the final enacted text must be reviewed; no enactment is assumed.
flags.action: Re-check File #261020 and obtain advice before issuing any banked-increase notice, including notices at or below 10% if other capital-improvement increases may apply. A notice served now could be affected if the proposal becomes law as currently described.

flags.item: Whether a §6.14 notice was served on the occupant who joined Unit 1 in April 2026
flags.detail: Under Rent Board Rules §6.14(b), for a co-occupant (someone with a direct rental agreement with the owner), a 6.14 notice must be served within a reasonable time after actual knowledge; failing to serve within 60 days establishes a rebuttable presumption of untimeliness. The reported change was 1 April 2026, so that sixty-day benchmark fell around 31 May 2026. By contrast, if the incoming occupant is NOT a co-occupant (a subtenant/roommate without a direct agreement), §6.14(c) governs post-April 25, 2000 departures and focuses on whether the landlord waives a reset by failing to serve an increase or reservation of rights within 90 days after written notice or actual knowledge that the last original occupant vacated (whereas §6.14(d) applies only to pre-April 25, 2000 departures). No notice, proof of service, or record of non-service was supplied for review.
flags.effect: If the incoming occupant is treated as a co-occupant and the owner later wants the §6.14(b) route when the last original occupant vacates, an untimely notice may bar it. If the occupant is a post-1996 subtenant (not a co-occupant), §6.14(c) and Civil Code §1954.53(d) have separate waiver and notice standards.
flags.action: Locate any 6.14 notice and its proof of service, or record the date the owner first learned of the occupancy and why no notice was served.

flags.item: Whether the occupant who joined Unit 1 in April 2026 is a co-tenant or a subtenant
flags.detail: Costa-Hawkins does not reach a co-tenant who moved in after the original occupant, regardless of when they moved in; a co-tenant is someone with an oral or written agreement with the landlord, or whom the landlord has treated as a tenant by the acceptance of rent or other conduct. A 6.14 notice, by contrast, can be served on either a subtenant or a co-tenant.
flags.effect: The label does not change the current 1.6% scenario, but it decides whether any later market-rate reset is available and by which route.
flags.action: Check whether the April 2026 instrument added the occupant to the lease, and whether rent has been accepted directly from them.

occupancy_rows.situation: An original occupant is still in the unit
occupancy_rows.rule: Both routes are keyed to the last original occupant leaving. Section 6.14 requires that the last original occupant "vacate"; Costa-Hawkins requires that the last original occupant no longer "permanently reside" in the unit.
occupancy_rows.effect: On the reported facts one original Unit 1 occupant remained after 1 April 2026, so no market-rate reset is available and the 1.6% allowance governs. Continuous occupancy still needs documents (H-06).

occupancy_rows.situation: A new occupant joined while an original occupant remained
occupancy_rows.rule: A landlord may not charge more rent solely because an additional occupant joined, even if the lease or rental agreement provides for the additional charge.
occupancy_rows.effect: Unit 1 is reported at $3,995.00 both before and after the 1 April 2026 change. That is consistent with the rule and must not change simply because occupancy changed.

occupancy_rows.rule: Under Rent Board guidance and Rules §6.14(b), a 6.14 notice on a co-occupant must be served within a reasonable time after actual knowledge of the occupancy (60 days establishes a rebuttable presumption). For a non-co-occupant subtenant where the last original occupant vacates on or after April 25, 2000, Rules §6.14(c) turns on post-vacancy waiver—such as failing within 90 days of written notice or actual knowledge to serve an increase or reserve rights (§6.14(d) covers pre-April 25, 2000 departures).
occupancy_rows.effect: The reported change was 1 April 2026, so the sixty-day benchmark fell around 31 May 2026, before this review. Whether a notice was served, and whether any presumption can be rebutted, is a private fact (H-23).

occupancy_rows.rule: Where an occupant is a post-1996 lawful subtenant or assignee (not a co-tenant), Civil Code §1954.53(d) and Rules §6.14(c)/(d)(2) permit establishing a new base rent when the last original occupant no longer permanently resides, even without an initial 6.14 notice, unless waived.
occupancy_rows.effect: A missed or late 6.14 notice does not by itself end the analysis. Costa-Hawkins has its own limits, including that it does not reach a co-tenant who moved in after the original occupant (H-24).

occupancy_rows.rule: A co-tenant is not subject to a Costa-Hawkins increase regardless of when the co-tenant moved in. A co-tenant is someone with an oral or written agreement with the landlord, or whom the landlord has treated as a tenant by the acceptance of rent or other conduct. A 6.14 notice, by contrast, can be served on either a subtenant or a co-tenant.
occupancy_rows.effect: If the incoming Unit 1 occupant was added to the lease, or the owner has accepted rent directly from them, they may be a co-tenant. That status is a private fact and changes which route, if any, is available later (H-24).

occupancy_rows.situation: No pre-filing is required for either route
occupancy_rows.rule: A landlord is not required to file a petition for approval of a §6.14 or Costa-Hawkins increase, but may file for a determination; a tenant may file a petition alleging an unlawful rent increase.
occupancy_rows.effect: If either route is ever relied on, the optional determination petition is a way to test it before serving. This dashboard does not establish that either route is available here.

occupancy_rows.situation: Effect on the annual and banked scenarios
occupancy_rows.rule: None of the above changes the 1.6% annual allowance while the current tenancies continue. It only matters if the last original occupant later leaves.

state_local_qa.question: Does a 2023 law require me to inform the San Francisco Rent Board about each rent increase on a rent-controlled unit — and is it state or local law?
state_local_qa.answer_short: It is local San Francisco law — not state law — and it is an annual report, not a per-increase filing.
answer_detail: The San Francisco Rent Ordinance (Chapter 37 of the San Francisco Administrative Code) requires owners of units subject to Chapter 37 to report information about each unit to the Rent Board on the Housing Inventory form, and a landlord must have a current rent increase license on file before any annual or banked rent increase goes into effect. For units in buildings with fewer than 10 units — including this reported two-unit building — reporting commenced March 1, 2023 and is updated annually by March 1 [S35] [S01] [S03].

California has no statewide rent board, and no California statute requires a landlord to notify or file with a rent board before raising rent. SB 567 (Durazo, chaptered September 30, 2023) amends Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12 — the just-cause termination and rent-cap provisions — including a duty to notify tenants of those rights, and it expressly does not preempt local rent control [S34]. The state notice rule (Civil Code section 827) requires written notice to the tenant — 30 days at 10 percent or less, 90 days above 10 percent — plus five calendar days for California mail: notice to the tenant, not a filing with any board [S08] [S21].

What this means for these units: there is no Rent Board application for approval of an ordinary annual or banked increase, no per-increase notice to the Board, and no state rent increase licence. The steps are: report or update the Housing Inventory each year by March 1; hold a current licence when the increase takes effect (generated after reporting, free); then serve a conforming written notice to the tenant [S03] [S01] [S05]. Coverage, current licences, ledgers, and lease status remain blank and flagged — see Flagged for Review.

Scope limits: this answers the state-versus-local question only. It does not confirm coverage, current licences, ledgers, or lease status — those remain blank and flagged (H-02, H-04, H-05, H-17, H-18).

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Confirm both units have current rent increase licences on the effective date — check the Rent Board Portal before serving notice and again on the effective date, and save dated evidence.
decision_suggestions.why: An increase effective while unlicensed is null and void; late reporting restores the licence only prospectively.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: Licence suspension and restoration; licence required on the effective date; no per-increase Board approval.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Read Unit 1's April 1, 2026 instrument (fixed term, month-to-month, escalation clause) before choosing any effective date.
decision_suggestions.why: Rent cannot be increased during a fixed term unless the agreement permits it; Unit 1's instrument is not supplied.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: State fixed-term guidance; Unit 1 fixed-term status unknown.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Rebuild Unit 2's bank from the full rent ledger and every increase notice since June 1, 2019 before using any banked amount.
decision_suggestions.why: The 13.1 percent illustration assumes no intervening increase — an arithmetic assumption, not an established fact.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: Banked increases must be calculated correctly from the actual history; no compounding or rounding up.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Re-check Board of Supervisors File #261020 and the Rent Board warning before noticing any banked or capital-improvement catch-up.
decision_suggestions.why: If enacted as proposed, the 10 percent cap would apply to banked increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026; it is pending, not law.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: Legistar record; Rent Board November 9, 2026 warning.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Re-check Form 571 after March 1, 2027 for the 2027-28 rate; never use an unpublished percentage.
decision_suggestions.why: The 1.6 percent allowance expires February 28, 2027; the next rate is blank until published.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Decide the path in writing before serving: raise neither unit; raise Unit 1 only (annual-only once the lease and licence are confirmed); raise Unit 2 only (annual-only once the current base is verified); or raise both on the same verified schedule.
decision_suggestions.why: Documented neutral reasons reduce — but do not eliminate — discrimination or retaliation exposure; identical treatment is not a safe harbour.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: FEHA, the Fair Housing Act, section 37.10B harassment, and section 1942.5 retaliation screening.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Obtain independent review of the draft notice (Rent Board counseling or an attorney or advocate); arithmetic alone is not a legal clearance.
decision_suggestions.why: Tenants can petition without a lawyer; the referral listing does not guarantee free representation.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: Rent Board counseling line and referral resources; petition without counsel.

decision_suggestions.suggestion: Keep a dated evidence file: lease, full ledger, every notice, proof of service, licence confirmation, and the calculation worksheet.
decision_suggestions.why: Every review check above depends on records that are not yet in the file.
decision_suggestions.official_basis: Notice contents, banking documentation, and repair-petition rules.
